items.q: Why is a well-known recipe less scarce than the flour used to bake it?
options: A recipe takes no time or effort to invent at first
Flour is a free good, so it has no price
Many can use it at once without using it up
Flour is a form of capital
Recipes are produced by the government

why.correct: Using flour uses it up, but one baker following a recipe does not stop another from following it too. Knowledge like this is not scarce in the usual way.
options: Inventing a recipe takes time and effort; what matters is that using it does not use it up.
Flour has a price because it is scarce; the recipe is the one that many can use at once without using it up.
Right: shared use does not use it up.
Flour is an ingredient used up in baking, not a tool or machine, and that is not the reason anyway.
Recipes come from many people, and who made one does not matter here.

items.q: A billionaire has more money than she could ever spend. Does she face scarcity?
options: Yes: her time is still limited
No: with enough money nothing is scarce
No: scarcity is a problem that firms face, not people
Yes, but just in years when prices are rising
No: scarcity ends once wants are met by income

why.correct: Money does not create more hours in a day. Every choice of how to spend her time still gives something up.
options: Right: time is scarce for everyone.
Money cannot buy more hours, so some choices still give things up.
Households and governments face scarcity too.
Scarcity does not depend on the price level.
Her wants and her time still outrun what she has; scarcity applies to every person, firm and society, whatever its income.

items.q: Which statement compares market and command economies accurately?
options: Market economies face scarcity and command economies do not
Command economies coordinate by prices; markets by plans
Command economies get by without any prices
Market economies get by without any government
Markets coordinate by prices; command economies by plans

why.correct: Both face scarcity and both have prices and governments; the difference is who decides and what coordinates the decisions.
options: Scarcity is universal.
That is reversed: markets coordinate through prices, and command economies through a central plan.
Command economies set prices by plan rather than letting markets set them.
Every real market economy has a government that enforces contracts and property rights.
Right: prices versus plans.

items.q: A software studio finds that each extra app it builds costs it fewer games than the last, because its team gets faster at apps. What shape would its PPC have?
options: Bowed out from the origin: increasing opportunity cost
A straight line: constant opportunity cost
Bowed out, because apps are easier to build than games
A vertical line
Bowed in: decreasing opportunity cost

why.correct: When each extra unit costs less of the other good, the opportunity cost is decreasing, which bows the curve in. This is the less common case.
options: Bowed out goes with each unit costing MORE.
A straight line goes with an unchanging cost.
Getting faster at apps lowers the games given up per app, which is decreasing opportunity cost: a PPC bowed in, not out.
A vertical line would mean no games could be traded for apps.
Right: decreasing cost bows the curve in.

items.q: A PPC is a straight line. What does that shape mean?
options: The opportunity cost rises with each extra unit
Resources are equally useless for both goods
The opportunity cost falls with each extra unit
Each extra unit costs the same amount
There is no opportunity cost

why.correct: A straight line has one slope, so each extra unit of one good costs the same amount of the other.
options: Rising cost bows the curve out.
A straight PPC means resources are equally suited to both goods, so each extra unit has the same opportunity cost.
Falling cost bows the curve in.
Right: constant opportunity cost.
Any downward-sloping PPC shows a cost.

items.q: A lawyer types faster than her assistant. Why might she still pay the assistant to do her typing?
options: She has the comparative advantage in typing
Her assistant has the absolute advantage in typing
She has the absolute advantage in legal work too, so she types
Typing costs her valuable legal work
Typing has no opportunity cost

why.correct: Her opportunity cost of typing is the legal work she gives up, which is high. The assistant gives up much less, so the assistant has the comparative advantage in typing.
options: Her opportunity cost of typing is the higher one, so the assistant has the comparative advantage.
She types faster, so SHE has the absolute advantage.
Absolute advantage does not decide who should type; her time typing costs her legal work, so the assistant has the comparative advantage.
Right: her opportunity cost of typing is high.
Every hour spent typing gives up some other use.

items.q: A baker owns her shop building outright. She could rent it to another business for $1,500 a month. How does using it for her bakery count?
options: As no cost, because she owns it
As a sunk cost she can ignore
As an explicit cost of $1,500 a month
As a benefit of $1,500 a month
As an implicit cost of $1,500 a month

why.correct: She pays no rent, but she gives up $1,500 a month she could earn renting it out: an implicit cost.
options: Owning it does not make its use free; the forgone rent is a cost.
The rent she gives up is a cost she pays every month she keeps the shop, so it is an implicit cost, not a sunk one.
She writes no rent check, so it is not explicit.
Rent she does not collect is a cost, not a benefit.
Right: a payment given up, not paid.

items.q: What does diminishing marginal utility mean?
options: Each extra unit costs more than the last
Total utility falls as you consume more
The price of a good falls as you buy more
Each extra unit adds less utility
Utility is the same for each unit

why.correct: Marginal utility falls with each unit, but as long as it is positive, total utility still rises.
options: That describes rising marginal cost; diminishing marginal utility is about satisfaction: each extra unit adds less.
Total utility keeps rising while marginal utility is positive.
This is about satisfaction, not prices.
Right: the extra satisfaction shrinks.
That would be constant marginal utility.

items.q: Lena buys her third slice of pizza only if the price falls, because the third slice satisfies her less than the second. Which idea explains why her demand curve slopes down?
options: Her rising cost of making pizza at home
The income effect of a higher income
A change in the price of a substitute
More buyers in the pizza market
Diminishing marginal utility

why.correct: Diminishing marginal utility: each extra slice adds less satisfaction, so Lena will buy more only at a lower price.
options: The idea is about Lena’s extra satisfaction from each slice, not a cost; falling marginal utility explains why she pays less for the third.
Her income did not change; the extra slice is simply worth less.
No other good's price changed here.
This is one buyer's choice, not the number of buyers.
Right: each extra slice is worth less to her.

items.q: Which statement is the law of demand?
options: Other things equal, a higher price raises the quantity demanded
Demand rises when the number of sellers rises
Other things equal, a higher price lowers the quantity demanded
Buyers want more of a good at each price when their incomes rise
Other things equal, a higher income lowers the quantity demanded

why.correct: The law of demand: other things equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises.
options: That is backward: buyers want less at a higher price.
Sellers affect supply, not the law of demand.
Right: price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
That describes a normal good, not the law of demand.
The law of demand links a good’s own price to its quantity demanded; income shifts demand instead.

items.q: A farmer can plant corn or soybeans on the same land. The price of soybeans rises sharply. What happens to the farmer's supply of corn?
options: It shifts right because farming pays more
Quantity of corn supplied rises along the curve
It shifts right as the farmer earns more from soybeans
It shifts left as land moves to soybeans
It does not change because corn's price is the same

why.correct: Soybeans are another good the same land can produce. When soybeans pay more, the farmer switches land to them, so she offers less corn at each price: the supply of corn shifts left.
options: Only soybeans pay more; corn now uses land that could earn more elsewhere.
The price of corn did not change.
A higher soybean price makes corn the costlier use of the land, so the farmer supplies less corn at each price.
Right: the price of another good the seller can make rose.
The price of a related good the seller can produce shifts supply.

items.q: A demand curve is a straight line sloping down. How does the price elasticity of demand change as you move down the line from high prices to low prices?
options: It falls at first and then rises again near the bottom
It stays the same, because the slope is the same
It rises, from inelastic at high prices to elastic at low prices
It falls, from elastic at high prices to inelastic at low prices
It is unit elastic at each point on the line

why.correct: The slope is the same everywhere, but elasticity falls: at high prices a small quantity makes any change a large percent, so demand is elastic; past the midpoint it is inelastic. The midpoint is unit elastic.
options: Along a straight downward demand line the elasticity falls steadily as the price falls; it does not turn back up.
Slope is not elasticity; percent changes differ along the line.
That is backward: the top of the line is the elastic part.
Right: same slope, changing percent changes.
Only the midpoint is unit elastic.

items.q: How is the price elasticity of demand calculated?
options: Percent change in price divided by percent change in quantity demanded
Change in quantity demanded divided by change in price
Price times quantity demanded
Percent change in total revenue divided by percent change in price
Percent change in quantity demanded divided by percent change in price

why.correct: Price elasticity of demand is the percent change in quantity demanded divided by the percent change in price, read as an absolute value.
options: That is upside down.
That is a slope-style ratio of units; elasticity uses percents.
That is total revenue.
The total revenue test uses elasticity, but the elasticity itself is the percent change in quantity demanded over the percent change in price.
Right: quantity on top, in percent.

options: 0.5; demand is inelastic, so total revenue rises
2; demand is elastic, so total revenue rises
2; demand is elastic, so total revenue falls
20; demand is elastic, so total revenue falls
1; demand is unit elastic, so total revenue is unchanged

Right: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{20\%}{10\%} = 2</annotation></semantics></math>, above 1, and revenue falls from $1,000 to $880.
That is the change in planners (20) per dollar of price, a slope, not an elasticity, which compares percent changes.
Quantity fell by 20% while the price rose by 10%, so the ratio is 2, not 1, and revenue changes.

items.q: Why does the supply of most goods become more elastic as sellers have more time to respond to a price change?
options: Buyers find more substitutes over time
Prices fall over time, so sellers produce more
Workers, machines and plants take time to add
Sellers face less competition as time passes
Sellers forget the old price

why.correct: With more time, sellers can hire and train workers, buy and install machines and build new plants, and new sellers can start up, so a price rise draws a larger increase in output.
options: That makes demand more elastic, not supply.
By the law of supply, lower prices lower quantity supplied.
Right: capacity grows with time.
Competition is not the reason; over time firms can add workers, machines and plants, so output responds more.
Supply elasticity is about the ability to change output.

items.q: Why must you keep the sign for income and cross-price elasticity but read the absolute value for price elasticity of demand?
options: Their sign tells the type of good or relationship; price elasticity's sign does not
Income and price changes are positive, so their elasticities are too
Income and cross-price elasticities are smaller than 1
Price elasticity of demand is larger, so its sign is dropped
The sign shows whether demand is elastic

why.correct: For price elasticity of demand the sign is always negative by the law of demand, so only the size carries information. For income and cross-price elasticity the sign is the information: normal or inferior, substitutes or complements.
options: Right: the sign carries the meaning for income and cross-price elasticity.
Income and cross-price elasticities can be negative.
The size does not decide it: the sign of income and cross-price elasticity names the kind of good or relationship, so it is kept.
Size is not why the sign is dropped.
Elastic or inelastic is read from the size, compared with 1.

options: That is the cross-price elasticity; a response to pay is the income elasticity, the percent change in quantity over the percent change in income.
That is upside down.
Right: the income elasticity of demand, quantity on top.
That is the price elasticity of demand.
Elasticity uses percent changes in quantity.

items.q: A frost cuts the coffee harvest and the price of coffee rises. Coffee growers in other regions plant more coffee trees, and some cafes switch to tea. What role is the higher price playing?
options: A rule the government uses to ration the coffee
A signal steering growers and buyers
A cost that shifts demand for coffee to the right
A price that growers set and buyers accept
A sign that the market has stopped working

why.correct: The price is a signal: it tells growers to send more land and labor to coffee and tells buyers to economize on it. Price signals allocate scarce resources toward where they are most valued.
options: No one set this price; it rose in the market and signals growers to plant more and buyers to use less.
Right: prices carry information and incentives.
A higher price moves buyers along demand; it does not shift it.
The price comes from the market, not from one side.
The market is responding as markets do, through the price.

items.q: Demand for two goods rises by the same amount. Good X has very inelastic supply; good Y has very elastic supply. Which statement is correct?
options: The quantities of X and Y rise by the same amount
The price of X rises more than the price of Y
The quantity of X rises more than the quantity of Y
The price of Y rises more than the price of X
Both prices rise by the same amount

why.correct: With inelastic supply, sellers cannot add much output, so most of the demand increase shows up as a higher price. With elastic supply, output rises a lot and the price only a little.
options: Elastic supply lets Y's output rise a lot, while X's inelastic supply sends most of its demand increase into price, so the quantity of Y rises more.
Right: inelastic supply pushes the change into price.
Inelastic supply limits how much X sellers can add.
Elastic supply lets Y sellers meet the demand with more output.
The size of the price change depends on the elasticity of supply.

items.q: A government limits the number of fishing licenses, so the yearly catch of a fish falls from the market quantity of 900 tons to 600 tons. Other things equal, what happens in the fish market?
options: The quantity falls to 600 tons and the price falls
The price stays the same because demand is unchanged
The quantity falls to 600 tons and the price rises
The quantity rises because each boat fishes more
The price falls to the level of 600 tons on supply

why.correct: A binding limit on quantity (a quota) holds the quantity below equilibrium. With fewer fish sold, buyers bid the price up along demand: the price rises and the quantity falls to 600 tons, and the units no longer traded are deadweight loss.
options: Less fish for the same buyers pushes the price up.
A lower quantity moves buyers up along demand to a higher price.
Right: a binding quota cuts quantity and raises the price.
The licenses limit the total catch.
Cutting the quantity to 600 tons moves the market up the demand curve, so buyers pay a higher price, not a lower one.

items.q: The graph shows a binding price ceiling on apartment rents. Which areas are the deadweight loss of the ceiling?
options: Area d
Areas c and e
Areas a, b and d
Area f
Areas d and e

why.correct: At the ceiling, landlords supply less than the equilibrium quantity, so fewer apartments are rented. The surplus on the units no longer traded, between demand and supply from the quantity supplied out to the old equilibrium quantity, is lost: areas c and e.
options: Area d moves from landlords to renters at the lower price; it is a transfer, not a loss.
Right: the triangle between demand and supply on the units the ceiling stops from being rented.
That is consumer surplus with the ceiling: renters keep a and b and gain d.
That is producer surplus with the ceiling.
That is what landlords lose; d goes to renters, so only e of it is deadweight loss, and c is lost from renters’ side.

items.q: How does a tariff on imports compare with an import quota that allows the same amount of imports?
options: A tariff raises imports; a quota lowers them
A quota lowers the domestic price; a tariff raises it
A tariff creates a deadweight loss, but a quota does not create one
Same price and imports; only a tariff gives the government revenue
A quota raises imports above free trade; a tariff lowers them

why.correct: Both raise the domestic price, raise domestic output, lower imports and create a deadweight loss. The difference is who gets the rectangle between the world price and the higher domestic price: with a tariff, the government collects it as revenue; with a quota, it goes to whoever holds the right to import.
options: A tariff raises the domestic price, so quantity supplied rises and quantity demanded falls: imports fall under a tariff too.
Both raise the domestic price.
Both cut trade below free trade, so both create deadweight loss.
Right: the revenue rectangle is the difference.
Both lower imports.

items.q: Next month Copperline doubles its presses to four and keeps six workers. What happens to the marginal product of the sixth worker?
options: It rises, because each worker now has more presses to work with
It falls, because diminishing marginal returns get stronger
It stays the same, because the number of workers did not change
It becomes zero, because the shop now has too many presses
It falls, because the shop now has more capital to pay for

why.correct: Marginal product depends on how much of the other inputs workers have. With four presses the sixth worker no longer waits in line, so the output that worker adds rises.
options: Right: more of the other input makes each worker more productive.
Diminishing returns come from crowding a fixed input; adding presses eases the crowding.
The workers are the same, but each now has more capital, so each can produce more.
Extra presses do not make a worker less productive.
The cost of presses does not set marginal product; with more presses per worker, each worker adds more output.

items.q: Which of these is a production function?
options: A list of the prices a firm charges for each product
A table of how many units buyers want at each price
The firm’s profit at each level of output
How much output each mix of inputs can make
A record of the firm's yearly spending on wages

why.correct: A production function describes the relationship between the inputs a firm uses (labor, capital, land) and the output it can produce.
options: Prices belong to demand and revenue, not to the production function.
That is a demand schedule.
Profit needs prices and costs; a production function links inputs to output only.
Right: a production function links inputs to output.
Spending is a cost; the production function is about physical output.

items.q: In the graph, MC slopes upward at larger outputs. Which idea best explains this?
options: The firm pays a larger fixed cost when it produces more
Diminishing marginal returns
Specialization makes each extra unit cheaper
Buyers are willing to pay less for more units
Average fixed cost rises as output grows

why.correct: With a fixed plant, the marginal product of labor eventually falls. Each extra unit then needs more labor hours, so marginal cost rises.
options: Fixed cost does not change with output, so it cannot make MC rise.
Right: when each worker adds less, each extra unit takes more paid work, so its cost rises.
Specialization lowers MC at small outputs; it does not explain the rise.
MC is a cost curve; buyers' willingness to pay does not set it.
AFC falls as output grows, and fixed cost does not affect MC; MC rises because each added worker adds less output.

items.q: Based on the table, what is Tellbrook's marginal cost of a chair when output rises from 20 to 30 chairs a week?

why.correct: Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the change in output: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>300</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>240</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{$300 - $240}{30 - 20}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= $6</annotation></semantics></math> a chair.
options: Right: $60 more cost spread over 10 more chairs.
That is the change in total cost; output rose by 10 chairs, so divide by 10.

That is average total cost at 30 chairs, <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>300</mn></mrow><mn>30</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{$300}{30}</annotation></semantics></math>, not marginal cost.

That is average total cost at 20 chairs, <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>240</mn></mrow><mn>20</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{$240}{20}</annotation></semantics></math>.

That is average variable cost at 30 chairs, <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>300</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><mn>30</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{$300 - $100}{30}</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Use the table. Buyers in the whole market want about 30,000 kayaks a year at a price near $6. About how many firms like this one can produce at the lowest long-run average total cost?
options: About 30 firms, each making 1,000 kayaks
About 5 firms, each making 6,000 kayaks
One firm, because one large firm has the lowest cost
About 300 firms, each making 100 kayaks
About 75 to 100 firms, each making 300 to 400 kayaks

why.correct: Minimum efficient scale is small (300 kayaks) next to the market (30,000), so many firms can each produce at the lowest average cost. A small minimum efficient scale relative to demand supports a market with many firms.
options: Lowest LRATC is at about 300 to 400 kayaks a year per firm, so 30,000 kayaks take about 75 to 100 such firms.
A firm making 6,000 kayaks would be far into diseconomies of scale, with high average cost.
LRATC rises past 400 kayaks, so one huge firm would have a higher average cost.
At 100 kayaks LRATC is $10, well above the lowest level.
Right: 30,000 / 400 = 75 and 30,000 / 300 = 100, so the market can hold many low-cost firms.

items.q: In one industry, minimum efficient scale is half of the quantity the whole market buys. Which market is most likely?
options: A market with hundreds of small firms
A market with a few large firms
A market with thousands of firms of many sizes
A market where firm size does not affect cost
A market where each firm makes one unit

why.correct: When minimum efficient scale is large compared with total demand, only a few firms can produce at the lowest cost, so the industry tends to have few, large firms.
options: Small firms would be far up the falling part of LRATC with high costs.
Right: at most two firms can each reach minimum efficient scale.
If the lowest-cost size is half the market, two or so firms can produce at minimum cost: a few large firms, not thousands.
This industry has large economies of scale, so size matters a great deal.
Tiny firms would have far higher average costs.

items.q: Why is a firm's economic profit never greater than its accounting profit?
options: It subtracts implicit costs too
Economic profit uses a lower revenue figure
Accounting profit adds the owner's forgone salary
It adds the value of the owner’s time to revenue
Economic profit counts fewer explicit costs

why.correct: Economic profit = accounting profit - implicit costs. Since implicit costs cannot be negative, economic profit is at most equal to accounting profit.
options: Right: subtracting more can only leave the same or less.
Both use the same total revenue.
Accounting profit leaves forgone salary out; it does not add it.
Economic profit subtracts the owner’s forgone earnings as an implicit cost; it does not add them to revenue.
Both subtract the same explicit costs.

items.q: Firms in the scooter-rental business are earning large economic profits. What is likely to happen next?
options: Current owners leave to find better uses of their time
The price rises as buyers compete for scooters
Accountants raise the firms' explicit costs
New scooter-rental firms are started
The firms' implicit costs fall to zero

why.correct: Positive economic profit means resources in this industry earn more than in their next-best use, which draws in new firms. Topic 3.6 follows what that does to price and profit.
options: They earn more here than elsewhere, so they have no reason to leave.
Economic profit draws new firms in, which adds supply and pushes the price down, not up.
Explicit costs depend on payments, not on profit.
Right: economic profit signals that resources earn more here than elsewhere.
Implicit costs depend on the owners' other choices, which have not changed.

items.q: What is normal profit?
options: The average accounting profit of firms in the industry
Any profit above the owner's explicit costs
Zero economic profit
A loss small enough that the firm keeps going
The profit left after implicit costs are added to revenue

why.correct: Normal profit is the return that just keeps the owner's resources in this business: zero economic profit.
options: Normal profit is defined by opportunity cost, not by an industry average.
That is accounting profit.
Right: the owner earns what the next-best use would pay.
Normal profit is not a loss; economic profit is exactly zero.
Implicit costs are subtracted, not added; normal profit is zero economic profit, which covers every cost including the owner’s best alternative.

items.q: In the graph, the price falls until the price line just touches the lowest point of ATC. The firm's best output now earns
options: a profit, because MR still equals MC
zero economic profit: price equals ATC
a loss equal to its fixed cost
a loss, because the price fell
a profit, because MC is below the price

why.correct: Where the price line touches the bottom of ATC, MR = MC there and P = ATC, so economic profit is zero: the break-even point.
options: MR = MC gives the best output, but at that output P = ATC, so profit is zero.
Right: P = ATC, so revenue just covers every cost, a normal profit.
With price at the lowest point of ATC, revenue covers every cost including fixed cost: zero economic profit, not a loss.
The price is still high enough to cover ATC at that output.
At the new best output MC equals the price.

items.q: Use the table. What is the firm's average revenue when it sells 5 mugs?
options: $20, the price of each mug
$100, the revenue from five mugs
$18.40, the cost of a mug on average
$8, the profit from five mugs
$1.60, the price minus the average cost

why.correct: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity. When every unit sells at the same price, AR = MR = P = $20.
options: Right: AR = TR / Q = 100 / 5 = 20, the price.
That is total revenue; divide by the five mugs.
That is average total cost (92 / 5).
That is profit, not revenue per mug.
$20 - $18.40 = $1.60 is the profit per mug; average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, $100 ÷ 5 = $20, the price.

items.q: A firm's rent goes up by $500 a month on a lease it cannot break. In the short run, how does this change its output decision?
options: It does not: rent is a fixed cost
It produces less, because its costs rose
It shuts down, because its loss is larger
It raises its price by the rent divided by output
It produces more to spread the rent over more units

why.correct: A fixed cost moves ATC, not MC or AVC. The firm still produces where MR = MC and still compares price with AVC; only its profit falls. In the long run, though, the higher rent counts.
options: Right: the output where MR = MC and the shutdown test stay the same.
The rent does not change the cost of an extra unit, so the best output is the same.
Shutting down still leaves the rent to pay; the AVC test is unchanged.
A competitive firm takes the price, and a fixed cost does not change MC, so neither price nor output changes in the short run.
Spreading the rent lowers AFC but does not change MC, so the best output stays put.

items.q: Based on the table, what should Wexford do in the short run?
options: Shut down; the $8 price does not cover its $9 ATC
Produce; it earns an economic profit of $50
Shut down; it loses $100 if it produces
Produce; it loses $50 instead of its $100 fixed cost
Produce more than 50 loads to spread its fixed cost

why.correct: At 50 loads Wexford loses <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">($8 - $9) \times 50 = -$50</annotation></semantics></math>. If it shut down it would still pay its fixed cost, <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">($9 - $7) \times 50 = $100</annotation></semantics></math>. The price is above AVC, so producing covers all variable cost and part of fixed cost: it loses $50 instead of $100.
options: With the price under ATC the firm makes a loss, but shutting down loses the whole $100 fixed cost; the test is price against AVC.
The price, $8, is below ATC, $9, so producing gives a loss of $50, not a profit.

Producing loses <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">($8 - $9) \times 50 = $50</annotation></semantics></math>; the $100 is what it loses if it shuts down.
Right: the price covers AVC, so producing loses less than shutting down.
Past 50 loads MC is above the price, so each extra load adds more to cost than to revenue.

items.q: The graph shows a perfectly competitive market (left) and one firm in it (right). Which describes the firm now and what happens in the long run?
options: It earns a profit, area a; firms exit until the price rises further
It earns a profit, areas a and b; firms enter until the price falls to minimum AVC
It breaks even; the market stays where it is in the long run
It makes a loss, area b; firms exit until the price rises to minimum ATC
It earns a profit, area a; firms enter until the price falls to minimum ATC

why.correct: The price is above the firm's ATC at the quantity where MR = MC, so the firm earns an economic profit, area a. Profit draws new firms in, market supply shifts right, and the price falls until it reaches the lowest point of ATC, where economic profit is zero.
options: Profit attracts firms; exit follows losses.
Areas a and b are total revenue, and entry stops at minimum ATC, where profit is zero, not at minimum AVC.
The price is above ATC at the firm's output, so there is a profit, area a, and that draws entry.
Area b is total cost; the price is above ATC, so the firm earns a profit, not a loss.
Right: entry shifts market supply right until profit is gone.

items.q: How does the marginal revenue curve of a firm with market power compare with that of a perfectly competitive firm?
options: It lies below demand, and so does a competitive firm’s MR
It lies below demand, while a competitive firm's MR equals its price
It lies on the demand curve, as it does for a competitive firm
It lies above the demand curve, while a competitive firm's MR is below it
It is horizontal, while a competitive firm's MR slopes down

why.correct: For a price taker, d = MR = AR = P: every unit adds its price to revenue. A price maker must cut the price on all units to sell one more, so its marginal revenue curve lies below its downward-sloping demand curve.
options: A competitive firm sells any amount at the market price, so its MR is the horizontal price line, not below its demand.
Right: the price cut on earlier units pulls MR below the price.
That holds only for a price taker, whose price does not fall as it sells more.
MR can never exceed the price for a firm that must cut its price to sell more.
That has the two firms the wrong way round.

items.q: Two new firms could make high-speed rail cars, but to reach a low average total cost a maker needs to produce for the whole national market. Why does this keep new firms out?
options: Diminishing marginal returns: each new firm adds less output
Economies of scale: a small entrant's ATC would be higher
The demand for rail cars is perfectly elastic
Rail cars are a public good, so no buyer pays for them
The firms already in the market earn zero economic profit

why.correct: Economies of scale: average total cost keeps falling as output grows, so one large firm can produce at a lower cost than a small entrant could. A newcomer would start with a higher ATC and could not match the price.
options: Diminishing returns describe one firm adding workers in the short run, not entry.
Right: falling long-run average total cost is a barrier to entry.
Perfectly elastic demand describes a price taker, not a market with one large producer.
Rail cars are rival and excludable; the barrier here is economies of scale, which give a small entrant a higher ATC.
Zero economic profit gives no reason to enter, but it is not a barrier that blocks entry.

items.q: Keeling Glassworks is the only maker of a special glass for telescopes. If it wants to sell more glass each month, it must
options: raise the price it charges
keep its price where it is, since demand does not depend on price
match the price of rivals in its market
lower the price it charges
raise its output while keeping its price

why.correct: A price maker faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so it sells more only by lowering its price: it chooses a price and quantity pair on its demand curve, not both freely.
options: A higher price moves it up its demand curve to a smaller quantity.
Buyers of the glass still buy less at a higher price.
It is the only maker; it has no rivals to match.
Right: on a downward-sloping demand curve, more is bought only at a lower price.
Its demand curve slopes down, so it can sell more only by lowering its price.

items.q: Which area is the monopolist's total revenue?
options: Area c
Areas a and b
Areas a, b and c
Areas a and c
Areas b and c

why.correct: Total revenue is price times quantity: the rectangle from the price down to the horizontal axis, out to the quantity sold. That is areas b and c (profit plus total cost).
options: Area c alone is total cost: ATC times quantity.
Area a is above the price; it belongs to buyers.
That adds consumer surplus, which the firm does not collect.
Area a is consumer surplus, above the price; total revenue is price times quantity, areas b and c.
Right: price times quantity, which is profit plus total cost.

items.q: Compared with the unregulated outcome, what does the socially optimal price of $2 do?
options: Raises rides and leaves the ferry with zero economic profit
Lowers the price and leaves the ferry with a profit
Lowers rides, because the price is below the ferry's cost
Leaves rides unchanged and moves profit to riders
Raises rides to the efficient quantity, but leaves the ferry with a loss

why.correct: At P = MC the ferry carries 8,000 rides instead of 4,000, the allocatively efficient quantity, so the deadweight loss is gone. But price is below ATC, so the ferry makes a loss unless it is subsidized.
options: Zero economic profit happens at the fair-return price ($4), where P = ATC.
At the socially optimal price, P = MC, which is below ATC for a natural monopoly, so the ferry runs at a loss.
A lower price ceiling on a monopolist raises quantity, up to where demand meets MC.
Quantity rises from 4,000 to 8,000 rides when the price falls to MC.
Right: P = MC is allocatively efficient, but below ATC.

items.q: A monopolist is producing where marginal revenue is $12 and marginal cost is $8. To raise profit it should
options: produce less and raise its price
keep its output and raise its price
shut down, since price is above marginal cost
produce more and raise its price
produce more and lower its price

why.correct: The next unit adds $12 to revenue and only $8 to cost, so producing more adds $4 to profit. Expanding output means lowering the price along demand until MR falls to MC.
options: Cutting output would give up units that add more to revenue than to cost.
With the same demand curve, a higher price means fewer sales.
Price above MC is normal for a monopolist; it is no reason to shut down.
Moving down its demand curve to sell more means a lower price, not a higher one.
Right: MR > MC, so each extra unit adds to profit.

items.q: Kestrel is a profit-maximizing monopoly. Based on the table, how many visits does it sell, and at what price?
options: 4 thousand visits at $4
4 thousand visits at $7
5 thousand visits at $6
3 thousand visits at $8
2 thousand visits at $9

why.correct: Total revenue is $10, $18, $24, $28 and $30 thousand, so marginal revenue is $10, $8, $6, $4 and $2 a visit. MR = MC = $4 at 4 thousand visits, and the price is read from demand at that quantity: $7.
options: The quantity is right, but $4 is marginal cost; the monopoly charges what buyers will pay, read from demand.
Right: MR = MC at 4 thousand visits, and demand gives the price there.
Total revenue is largest there, but the fifth thousand adds $2 of revenue and $4 of cost.
The fourth thousand visits add $4 of revenue and $4 of cost, so the park goes on to 4 thousand.
The third and fourth thousand visits each add at least as much revenue as cost, so stopping at 2 gives up profit.

items.q: The graph shows a natural monopoly. A regulator wants more output than the unregulated monopoly makes, without the firm needing a subsidy to stay in business. Which price should it set?
options: The price where demand crosses MC, the socially optimal price
The price on demand above the quantity where MR = MC
The price where ATC reaches its lowest point
The price where demand crosses ATC, the fair-return price
The price where marginal revenue equals zero

why.correct: Where demand crosses ATC (the fair-return price), price equals average total cost, so the firm earns zero economic profit and needs no subsidy, and output is larger than where MR = MC. Where demand crosses MC, output is larger still, but ATC falls over the whole range of demand and lies above MC there, so the firm would make a loss.
options: That gives the efficient quantity, but ATC is above MC there, so the firm makes a loss and needs a subsidy.
That is the unregulated monopoly price; the regulator wants more output than that.
ATC keeps falling over the whole range of demand, so it has no lowest point there.
Right: P = ATC gives zero economic profit and more output than at MR = MC.
That maximizes total revenue; it still leaves a profit and gives less output than the fair-return price.

items.q: What does a monopolistically competitive firm have in common with a monopolist?
options: Barriers that keep new firms out
Zero economic profit in the short run
A downward-sloping demand curve
Positive economic profit in the long run
A product with no close substitutes

why.correct: Both face a downward-sloping demand curve, so both have MR below demand and charge a price above MC. They differ in entry: easy in monopolistic competition, blocked in monopoly.
options: Entry is easy in monopolistic competition.
Short-run profit can be positive for both; what they share is a downward-sloping demand curve.
Right: both are price makers.
Entry drives a monopolistic competitor's profit to zero.
Monopolistic competitors sell close, though not identical, substitutes.

items.q: A dominant strategy is a strategy that
options: contains the largest single payoff in the matrix
gives the two players the largest combined payoff
the player chooses after first seeing what the rival did
beats its other strategies whatever the rival does
the rival is most likely to choose

why.correct: A dominant strategy gives a player a higher payoff than any other strategy, whatever the other player chooses. It is proved with one comparison for each of the other player's choices.
options: A large payoff in one cell does not make a strategy better against each choice of the rival.
That is the joint-profit cell, which is a different idea.
In these games the players choose at the same time.
Right: it wins against each choice of the rival.
A dominant strategy is about the player’s own payoffs: it does better than its other strategies whatever the rival does.

items.q: Based on the payoff matrix, which statement about dominant strategies is correct?
options: Altura's dominant strategy is to advertise; Bexley has no dominant strategy
Both gyms have a dominant strategy to advertise
Neither gym has a dominant strategy
Both gyms have a dominant strategy not to advertise, where joint profit is 90
Bexley's dominant strategy is to advertise; Altura has no dominant strategy

why.correct: Altura: if Bexley advertises, 30 > 20; if Bexley does not, 50 > 45. Advertising is better either way, so it is Altura's dominant strategy. Bexley: if Altura advertises, advertising is better (25 > 15); if Altura does not, not advertising is better (45 > 40). Bexley's best choice depends on Altura, so Bexley has no dominant strategy.
options: Right: Altura compares 30 > 20 and 50 > 45; Bexley's best choice changes with Altura's.
Bexley does better not advertising (45 > 40) when Altura does not advertise, so advertising is not dominant for Bexley.
Altura is better off advertising whatever Bexley does: 30 > 20 and 50 > 45.
The cell with the largest combined payoff is not a dominant strategy; each gym compares its own payoffs.
That reverses the two: Altura's best choice is the same either way, Bexley's is not.

items.q: In the scenario, which later event would most likely lead the boatyards to want fewer welders?
options: More fishing crews move to Brackwater
A new road brings more buyers from other towns
The fish-processing plant closes and crews order fewer boats
The price of a new fishing boat rises
Welders find new tools that let them weld faster

why.correct: The demand for a factor is derived from the demand for the product. Less demand for boats means a lower price for boats and a lower MRP for each welder.
options: More crews would raise the demand for boats and so for welders.
More buyers raise the demand for boats and so for welders; the plant closing lowers boat demand and, through MRP, welder demand.
Right: lower demand for boats lowers the price of boats and the revenue each welder brings in, so the boatyards want fewer welders.
A higher boat price raises the revenue each welder's work brings in, so boatyards want more welders.
Faster welding raises each welder's marginal product, so each welder is worth more to a boatyard.

items.q: Which of these is a transaction in a factor market?
options: A bakery sells a cake to a café
A student buys a coffee at the café
A café sells gift cards to customers
A café hires a weekend barista
A family buys a used car from a neighbor

why.correct: In a factor market the firm is the buyer and the owner of labor, land or capital is the seller.
options: That is a product market sale; a factor market trades inputs such as labor, as when the café hires a barista.
Coffee is a product sold to a household.
That is a sale of the café's product.
Right: the café is buying labor, a factor of production.
A car bought for the family's own use is a consumer good.

items.q: In the graph, a single firm that hires developers pays the new wage set in the market. How does the firm's own MRP curve compare with before?
options: It is unchanged, because the firm makes the same number of apps
It has shifted right, because the wage is now lower
It has shifted right, because developers are easier to hire
It has become horizontal at the new wage
It has shifted left, because each developer's work brings in less revenue

why.correct: Market labor demand is the sum of firms' demands. It shifted left because each firm's MRP fell.
options: A lower product price lowers MR, so MRP = MP × MR falls even with the same MP.
A lower wage is a movement along a firm's MRP curve, not a shift of it.
MRP depends on marginal product and the product’s price; labor demand fell, so each developer’s MRP fell and the curve shifted left.
MRP slopes down because marginal product falls; the wage does not change its shape.
Right: the cause of the market shift, a lower product price, lowers MRP at each firm too.

items.q: The price of a machine that does the same job as forklift operators falls sharply. Assume warehouses replace operators with the machines. What happens to the wage and employment of forklift operators?
options: Both fall
Both rise
The wage rises and employment falls
The wage falls and employment rises
The wage falls and employment stays the same

why.correct: A cheaper substitute input lowers the demand for labor that does the same job.
options: Right: labor demand shifts left, down along labor supply.
Cheaper substitutes for workers lower the demand for those workers.
That pattern comes from a fall in labor supply.
That pattern comes from a rise in labor supply.
Cheaper substitute machines lower the demand for operators, so along an upward labor supply both the wage and employment fall.

items.q: A competitive firm's next worker has an MRP of $95. The market wage is $80. What should the firm do?
options: Not hire, because her MRP is below the MRP of earlier workers
Hire if the firm's total revenue is above its total cost
Hire her: she adds $15 more to revenue than to cost
Hire her if her MRP is above the average MRP
Hire her and pay her a wage of $95, her MRP

why.correct: Hire while MRP is at least MRC. Here $95 > $80.
options: Comparing with earlier workers does not matter; compare her MRP with the wage.
The decision is at the margin: $95 against $80.
Right: MRP > MRC, so hiring raises profit.
The rule is marginal: hire while MRP is at least MRC (the wage), and $95 is above $80.
A wage taker pays the market wage, $80; paying her full MRP would add nothing to profit.

items.q: Based on the table, how many bakers does Brindle hire to maximize profit?
options: 5 bakers
2 bakers
3 bakers
1 baker
4 bakers

why.correct: Marginal product is 10, 8, 6, 4 and 2 loaves, so MRP <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= MP \times $5</annotation></semantics></math> is $50, $40, $30, $20 and $10. Brindle hires while MRP is at least the $30 wage (its MRC): 3 bakers. The fourth adds $20 of revenue for $30 of cost.
options: That is where output is largest; the fourth and fifth bakers cost more than they add to revenue.
The third baker adds $30 of revenue for $30 of cost, so hiring her does not lower profit; MRP = MRC at 3.
Right: the third baker's MRP equals the $30 wage; the fourth's is $20.
That is the baker with the largest MRP, but the second and third also add at least their wage.

The fourth baker's MRP is <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4 \times $5 = $20</annotation></semantics></math>, less than the $30 wage.

items.q: In a perfectly competitive labor market, a minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage. How does its effect on employment differ from a minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage in a monopsony?
options: It raises employment, like the one in the monopsony
It lowers employment; the monopsony one raises it
It raises employment in both markets
Both lower employment
Neither changes employment

why.correct: The same policy can have opposite effects on employment depending on the market structure.
options: Above the competitive equilibrium, firms want fewer workers at the higher wage.
Right: in a competitive market, firms move up their labor demand and hire fewer; in the monopsony, MFC falls for the next workers.
In a competitive market a wage floor above equilibrium cuts the quantity of labor demanded, so employment falls there.
In the monopsony case, MFC for the next workers falls to the minimum wage, so employment rises.
Both binding wages change who is hired.

items.q: When the market quantity is below the efficient quantity, what is true of the next unit not produced?
options: Its MSB is below its MSC, so the quantity is right
Its MSC is greater than its MSB
Its MSB equals its MSC
Its MSB is greater than its MSC
Its MSB and MSC are both zero

why.correct: Underproduction leaves units with MSB > MSC unmade; that lost net benefit is the deadweight loss.
options: If MSB were below MSC the unit should not be made; below the efficient quantity, MSB is above MSC.
That describes units beyond the efficient quantity.
Equality holds only at the efficient quantity.
Right: society would gain by making it.
Neither is zero just because the unit is not made.

items.q: In the graph, which area is the deadweight loss?
options: Areas a, b and c
Area c
Area a
Areas b and c
Area b

why.correct: Deadweight loss counts only the units that should not be made, and only the amount by which their MSC exceeds their MSB.
options: Together these are the total external cost of every unit the market makes.
Area c lies between D and S beyond the efficient quantity; it is part of what buyers and sellers gain on those units.
Right: the triangle between MSC and D from the efficient quantity to the market quantity.
Those are external costs on units the efficient quantity keeps or that private surplus offsets; the deadweight loss is the triangle a.
Area b is the external cost of units that are worth making.

items.q: Getting a flu shot also protects people who do not get one. In the graph, which describes the market outcome and a policy that moves it to the efficient quantity?
options: Too many shots, with deadweight loss a; a per-unit tax equal to the external benefit
Too few shots, with deadweight loss a, b and c; a per-unit subsidy
The efficient quantity, so no policy is needed
Too few shots, with deadweight loss a; a price ceiling on flu shots
Too few shots, with deadweight loss a; a per-unit subsidy equal to the external benefit

why.correct: Buyers weigh only their own benefit (MPB), so the market makes the quantity where MPB meets supply, less than the efficient quantity where MSB = MSC. The shots not made would be worth more to society than they cost, so area a, between MSB and supply over those shots, is the deadweight loss. A per-unit subsidy equal to the external benefit per shot raises the quantity to the efficient one.
options: The market ignores the benefit to others, so it makes too few, not too many, and a tax would cut the quantity further.
Areas a, b and c are the external benefit; the deadweight loss is the triangle a, on the shots the market does not provide.
Buyers weigh only their own benefit, so the market quantity falls short of where MSB = MSC.
A ceiling lowers the quantity supplied, which moves output further from the efficient quantity; a subsidy raises it.
Right: the market leaves out the benefit to others, and a subsidy of that size corrects it.

items.q: The same toll road becomes badly congested at rush hour. How does that change its rivalry?
options: It becomes nonexcludable: drivers can no longer be stopped
Nothing changes: roads are nonrival
It becomes rival: each extra car slows the others
It becomes excludable, because tolls are charged
It becomes a public good

why.correct: Many goods are nonrival only up to a point. When crowded, they become rival.
options: The gate still works.
Rivalry depends on use; a crowded road is rival.
Right: congestion means one driver's use reduces the value to others.
A toll road was already excludable; congestion changes rivalry, since each extra car slows the others.
With a gate it stays excludable.

items.q: What does regulation of market power try to do?
options: Raise the profits of firms with market power
Set each price at the highest willingness to pay of any buyer
Move the firm toward competitive output and price
Keep firms from earning a normal profit
Keep firms from earning any accounting profit

why.correct: Price regulation, antitrust and similar policies aim at the inefficiency of market power: P > MC and too little output.
options: Regulation usually lowers monopoly profit.
That describes perfect price discrimination, not regulation.
Right: lower price, more output, less deadweight loss.
Fair-return regulation is designed to allow a normal profit.
Regulation aims at competitive price and output; firms can still earn an accounting profit and a normal profit.

items.q: A country makes its income tax more progressive and spends the revenue on transfer payments to low-income households. What happens to the Lorenz curve for income after taxes and transfers?
options: It moves away from the line of equality
It does not move, because total income is the same
It moves below the line of equality for the first time
It moves toward the line of equality
It becomes the line of equality

why.correct: Progressive taxes and transfers are the main policies that move the after-tax Lorenz curve toward equality.
options: Both changes narrow the gap between high and low incomes.
The curve shows shares, and the shares change.
A Lorenz curve already lies below the line of equality; more progressive taxes and transfers move it closer to the line.
Right: higher incomes keep a smaller share and lower incomes gain, so shares are more equal.
Shares become more equal, not exactly equal.

items.q: A student says, "My opportunity cost of studying tonight is the money I spent on my textbook." What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing: past spending is the opportunity cost
Studying has no opportunity cost
The cost is the textbook money plus her time tonight
The textbook money is gone either way; the cost is tonight's next-best use
The opportunity cost is the price of a brand-new copy of the textbook

why.correct: Opportunity cost looks forward: what you give up by choosing this over your next-best option now. Money already spent is not given up by tonight's choice.
options: Money spent in the past is not given up by a choice made now.
Every use of time gives up some other use.
Money already spent is a sunk cost: it is gone whatever she does tonight, so it is not part of the opportunity cost.
Right: it is the next-best use of the evening.
Buying a new book is not what tonight's choice gives up.

items.q: Why do well-defined property rights help a market economy work?
options: Owners keep what they earn, so they have reason to produce
They let the government set the prices of goods
They promise each firm that it will make a profit
They make each good free for the people who need it
They remove scarcity

why.correct: If you can keep the rewards of building or improving something, you have a reason to do it. Without secure ownership, that reason weakens.
options: Right: secure rewards create incentives.
Property rights let owners, not the government, decide.
Owners can still lose money; rights do not promise a profit.
Property rights do not make goods free; they let owners keep what they earn, which gives them a reason to produce and trade.
Scarcity remains in every system.

items.q: In a market economy, what mainly coordinates the choices of millions of buyers and sellers?
options: Prices
A central planning board
Laws that fix the output of each firm
Tradition passed down in families
Votes held for each good

why.correct: Prices carry information about what buyers want and what it costs to make, and they give people reasons to act on it.
options: Right: prices coordinate.
A planning board coordinates a command economy.
Fixing output by law is a command method; in a market economy prices coordinate buyers and sellers.
Tradition decided production in some older societies, not in a market economy.
Markets do not vote on each good.

items.q: A furniture maker spends this year building new machines instead of making as many chairs and tables as it could. What does this choice do to its PPC for chairs and tables in later years?
options: It shifts the curve in, because it made fewer chairs this year
It leaves the curve unchanged
It shifts the curve out: more capital
It moves the firm to a point inside the curve for good
It turns the curve into a straight line

why.correct: Giving up some output now to build capital adds to the firm's resources, so in later years it can make more of both goods: growth.
options: Making fewer chairs this year is a move along or inside this year's curve; it does not shrink later years' resources.
The firm has more machines, so its limits change.
Right: more capital means growth.
Building machines this year adds capital, so later the whole curve shifts out; producing inside the curve today is a choice, not a lasting effect.
The shape depends on how suited resources are, not on growth.

items.q: Two bakers have the same opportunity cost of a pie: 3 loaves of bread each. What can trade between them do?
options: The faster baker gains and the slower one loses
Both gain if the faster baker makes the pies
Both gain, as two producers do from any trade
The slower baker gains the most
Neither gains from trading

why.correct: Gains from trade come from different opportunity costs. With equal costs, there is no price between them that helps one without hurting the other.
options: Speed is absolute advantage; what matters is that the costs are equal.
With the same opportunity cost there is no comparative advantage, so specializing and trading creates no gain.
Gains need different opportunity costs.
With equal costs, neither has a cost advantage to trade on.
Right: equal costs leave no gain.

items.q: What does it mean to specialize?
options: To make a little of many goods yourself
To make each good you consume by yourself
To buy most goods from producers in other countries
To focus production on a few goods
To make the good with the highest price

why.correct: Specializing means focusing on what you make at a low opportunity cost and trading for the rest.
options: That is the opposite of specializing, which is focusing production on a few goods and trading for the rest.
Making everything yourself is the opposite of specializing.
Buying from others is trade; specializing is about what you make.
Right: focus on a few goods.
Specializing follows opportunity cost, not the highest price.

items.q: For a firm, what is the total benefit of producing and selling its goods?
options: The money it takes in from sales
The satisfaction its owner feels
The profit it earns after paying its costs
Its explicit costs
The number of workers it hires

why.correct: A firm's total benefit is its revenue: the money it receives from selling its output.
options: Right: revenue.
Satisfaction is how a consumer measures benefit.
Profit is benefit minus cost; the total benefit of selling is the revenue itself.
Costs are subtracted from benefit, not the benefit itself.
Hiring is part of cost, not benefit.

items.q: For Priya, the last book she buys gives 30 utils per dollar and the last concert ticket 18 utils per dollar, and she has spent her whole budget. How can she raise her total utility?
options: Spend more on concerts and less on books
Shift some money from concerts to books
Buy one more of each with money she saves
Keep the same bundle
Stop buying books

why.correct: A dollar moved from concerts to books loses about 18 utils and gains about 30. She should shift until the ratios are equal.
options: That moves money toward the LOWER MU per dollar.
Right: move money toward the higher MU per dollar.
Her whole budget is spent, so she has no money left over; she raises utility by moving dollars from concerts (18) to books (30).
Unequal ratios mean a better bundle exists.
Books give the most utility per dollar right now.

items.q: In Corvia, an invented country, new laws let people own and sell the apartments they live in, and owners can keep what they earn from a sale. What does this change most directly do?
options: It sets by law the price at which apartments are bought and sold
It gives people an incentive to buy, improve and trade apartments
It shifts demand for apartments left by adding rules
It raises the cost of building new apartments
It lowers the quantity of apartments buyers want

why.correct: Well-defined property rights let owners keep the gains from trading, which gives buyers and sellers the incentive to use a market. Clear ownership is what lets a market for apartments work.
options: Property rights decide who owns a thing, not what it sells for.
Right: owners can keep the gains from a trade.
Clear ownership makes buying more attractive, not less.
Property rights do not add a building cost; they let owners keep the gains from buying, improving and selling, which is the incentive.
Nothing here lowers what buyers want at a given price.

items.q: A bakery already uses its ovens all day. To bake more bread it must pay workers overtime and rent a second oven. Why does this make the supply curve slope up?
options: Buyers want fewer loaves when the price rises
The bakery’s fixed cost rises with each extra loaf
Overtime shifts the supply curve to the right
A higher price lowers the bakery's costs
Each extra loaf costs more, so a higher price is needed to offer more

why.correct: Producing more costs more for each extra loaf (overtime, a rented oven), so the bakery offers more loaves only at a higher price that covers that rising cost.
options: That is the law of demand, a buyer's choice.
Fixed cost does not change with output; the extra loaves cost more because overtime and a rented oven raise marginal cost.
Overtime makes extra output costlier; it does not raise supply.
The price does not change the cost of baking.
Right: the price must cover the rising cost of extra output.

items.q: Which statement is the law of supply?
options: Other things equal, a higher price raises the quantity demanded
A higher price lowers the quantity sellers offer
Supply rises when buyers' incomes rise
Other things equal, a higher price raises the quantity supplied
Sellers offer more when input prices rise

why.correct: The law of supply: other things equal, when a good's price rises, the quantity supplied rises, and when it falls, the quantity supplied falls.
options: That swaps the sides of the market; the law of supply is about the quantity sellers offer.
That is backward: sellers offer more at a higher price.
Income is a demand shifter.
Right: price and quantity supplied move together.
Higher input prices lower supply.

items.q: A movie theater sells a large popcorn at $9, with no other snack seller nearby. A month later a snack cart opens outside. What most likely happens to the price elasticity of demand for the theater's popcorn?
options: It falls, because popcorn is now easier to find
It rises, because buyers now have a substitute
It does not change, because the price is the same
It falls, because buyers now spend less on snacks
It becomes perfectly inelastic

why.correct: The cart offers a close substitute, so buyers can switch when the theater's price is high. More substitutes make demand more elastic.
options: More places to buy a similar snack make the theater's demand more elastic.
Right: substitutes make buyers more price sensitive.
Elasticity depends on substitutes, not just the current price.
A new substitute nearby makes buyers more willing to switch away when the theater’s price rises, so demand becomes more elastic.
A new substitute makes demand less inelastic, not more.

items.q: Which good is likely to have the least elastic supply over the next week?
options: Plastic cups made by machines that sit idle half the day
Paper napkins made in a plant with spare capacity
Canned beans stored in a large warehouse
Fresh fish from a small fleet
Digital music downloads

why.correct: Fresh fish spoils and the catch for the week is largely set by the boats already at sea, so sellers cannot add much quickly. Goods that are easy to store or to make from easy-to-buy inputs have more elastic supply.
options: Spare capacity makes supply elastic.
Spare capacity lets output rise quickly, so supply is elastic; a small fishing fleet cannot catch much more within a week.
Stored stock can be released when the price rises.
Right: perishable, with output that is hard to raise quickly.
An extra download costs almost nothing to supply.

items.q: How is the price elasticity of supply calculated?
options: Price divided by quantity supplied, at one point
Percent change in price divided by percent change in quantity supplied
Change in quantity supplied divided by change in price
Percent change in quantity demanded divided by percent change in price
Percent change in quantity supplied divided by percent change in price

why.correct: Price elasticity of supply is the percent change in quantity supplied divided by the percent change in price. Because the two move together, it is positive.
options: Elasticity compares two percent changes: the percent change in quantity supplied over the percent change in price.
That is upside down.
That uses units; elasticity uses percent changes.
That is the price elasticity of demand.
Right: quantity on top, in percent.

items.q: A rise in the price of gasoline lowers the quantity of large trucks bought. What does this say about the cross-price elasticity of demand for large trucks with respect to the price of gasoline?
options: It is positive, so the goods are complements
It is positive, so the goods are substitutes
It is negative, so the goods are substitutes
It is zero, so the goods are unrelated
It is negative, so the goods are complements

why.correct: The gasoline price went up and truck purchases went down: the changes have opposite signs, so the cross-price elasticity is negative. Gasoline and trucks are complements.
options: Gasoline up and trucks bought down gives a negative cross-price elasticity; a negative value means complements.
The quantity of trucks fell as the gasoline price rose: a negative sign.
Negative cross-price elasticity marks complements.
Truck purchases responded, so they are related.
Right: opposite directions give a negative sign.

items.q: Based on the table, and assuming nothing else changed, what is the income elasticity of demand for bus rides in Corran, and what kind of good are they?
options: -1; bus rides are an inferior good
1; bus rides are a normal good
-1; bus rides are a normal good
-10; bus rides are an inferior good
-5; bus rides are an inferior good

why.correct: Income rises <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1{,}100 - 1{,}000}{1{,}000} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 10\%</annotation></semantics></math> and rides fall <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>45</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><mn>50</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{45 - 50}{50} \times 100 = -10\%</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_I = \frac{-10\%}{10\%} = -1</annotation></semantics></math>. A negative income elasticity means an inferior good.
options: Right: rides fall as income rises, so the elasticity is negative.
That drops the sign; for income elasticity the sign is the answer, and it is negative here.
The number is right, but a negative income elasticity marks an inferior good.
That is the percent change in rides alone; divide it by the 10% change in income.
That is the change in rides, 5, not a percent change; elasticity compares percent changes.

items.q: A farmer would sell a bushel of apples for as little as $12 and sells it for $20. What is the farmer's producer surplus on that bushel?
options: $16, halfway between the two prices

why.correct: Producer surplus is the price received minus the lowest price the seller would accept: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">$20 - $12 = $8</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: That is the whole price, not the gain over the least the farmer would accept.
That is the least the farmer would accept.
Surplus is the difference, not the sum.
Right: $20 minus $12.
Producer surplus is the price received minus the least the seller would accept: $20 - $12 = $8.

items.q: What is market equilibrium?
options: The price at which sellers earn the most profit they can
The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
The quantity where buyers spend the most
The highest price any buyer would pay for the first unit
The quantity at which the government sets prices

why.correct: Market equilibrium is the price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied: where the demand and supply curves cross. At that price the market clears.
options: Equilibrium is about matching quantities, not sellers' best outcome.
Right: the market clears.
Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, not where spending is largest.
That is where demand starts on the price axis.
Equilibrium arises from buyers and sellers in a market.

items.q: At a price below the equilibrium price, which is true?
options: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: a surplus
Demand shifts left to meet supply
Supply shifts right to meet demand
The market clears at the lower price
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: a shortage

why.correct: Below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, a shortage. The shortage pushes the price up.
options: A surplus happens above the equilibrium price.
Disequilibrium changes the price, not the curves.
A price below equilibrium causes a movement along the curves, not a shift; quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
The market clears only at the equilibrium price.
Right: below equilibrium, a shortage.

items.q: A city sets a ceiling of $2.50 on a bus ticket when the market price is $2.00. What happens?
options: A shortage, because a ceiling holds the price down
The price rises to $2.50
A surplus, because sellers want to charge $2.50
A surplus of bus tickets, because buyers pay less
Nothing: the ceiling is above the equilibrium price

why.correct: A ceiling above the equilibrium price does not bind: the market already settles below it, so the price, quantity and surpluses are unchanged.
options: A ceiling holds the price down only when it sits below equilibrium.
A ceiling is a maximum, not a target.
At $2.00 the market already clears.
A ceiling above the market price does not bind, so the price stays at $2.00 with no shortage and no surplus.
Right: a nonbinding ceiling has no effect.

items.q: The graph shows a binding price floor on milk. Which areas are producer surplus with the floor?
options: Areas d, e and f
Areas b, d and f
Area f
Areas c and e
Area b

why.correct: With the floor, buyers pay the higher price and buy the smaller quantity, which is all sellers can sell. Producer surplus is above supply and below the floor price on those units: areas b, d and f. Area b is taken from buyers by the higher price.
options: That was producer surplus before the floor; area e is lost and area b is gained.
Right: above supply, below the floor, out to the quantity bought.
Area f is part of it, but sellers also keep d and gain b at the higher price.
That is the deadweight loss of the floor.
Area b is the part moved from buyers to sellers; producer surplus also includes d and f.

items.q: Why does a country that opens to trade import a good whose world price is below its own price?
options: Domestic farms are forced to stop producing
The government sets the world price below the domestic price
Its own producers have the absolute advantage
Imports raise the domestic price
Other producers make it at a lower opportunity cost

why.correct: Other countries can supply the good at a lower opportunity cost: they have a comparative advantage in it. Buying at the lower world price lets the country use its own resources where it has a comparative advantage.
options: Domestic farms keep producing up to where supply meets the world price.
The world price comes from the world market.
If domestic producers made it at lower cost the domestic price would be lower; it imports because others have the lower opportunity cost.
Imports at a lower world price lower the domestic price.
Right: comparative advantage drives trade.

items.q: Use the table. The owner leases a second field next season and can change the number of fields, pickers and crates. Which statement describes this decision?
options: It is a long-run decision, because each input can now change
It is a short-run decision, because the farm still has pickers
It shows diminishing marginal returns, because output per field falls
It is a short-run decision, because one field is still fixed
It changes nothing, because the number of pickers per field stays the same

why.correct: The short run has at least one fixed input (here, the one field). When the farm can change every input, including land, it is planning for the long run.
options: Right: once no input is fixed, the firm is in the long run.
Pickers can change in the short run too; what makes this long run is that the land can now change.
Diminishing marginal returns come from adding one input to a fixed input. Here no input is fixed.
With the lease the owner can change fields as well as pickers and crates; when every input can change, it is the long run.
Changing the amount of land is exactly what makes this a long-run choice.

items.q: At a bike repair shop, the marginal product of the next mechanic is below the current average product. If the shop hires that mechanic, average product will
options: fall, because the mechanic adds less than the average
rise, because total product rises
stay the same, because marginal product is still positive
rise, because the new mechanic adds to total output
fall to zero, because returns are diminishing

why.correct: Marginal product below average product pulls average product down, just as a test score below your average lowers your average.
options: Right: adding a value below an average pulls the average down.
Total product rises, but by less than the average, so output per worker falls.
A positive marginal product raises total product, but the average depends on how MP compares with average product.
Total product rises, but when the added output is below the average, the average is pulled down.
Average product falls a little; it does not drop to zero.

items.q: Based on the table, what is the marginal product of the third worker, and have diminishing marginal returns begun?
options: 26 bowls; diminishing marginal returns have begun
8 bowls; marginal returns are still increasing
10 bowls; marginal returns are still increasing
8 bowls; diminishing marginal returns have begun
8.7 bowls; diminishing marginal returns have begun

why.correct: Marginal product is the change in output from one more worker: 8, 10, 8, 6 and 4 bowls. The third worker adds <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>26</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">26 - 18 = 8</annotation></semantics></math> bowls, fewer than the second worker's 10, so diminishing marginal returns have begun.
options: That is total product with three workers, not the third worker's addition.
The number is right, but 8 is below the second worker's 10, so returns are now diminishing.
That is the second worker's marginal product.
Right: 8 is less than the second worker's 10.

That is average product, <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>26</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{26}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, not marginal product.

items.q: In the scenario, the price of flour rises. How does this change Pepperwood Bakery's cost curves?
options: MC, AVC and ATC shift up; AFC does not change
AFC shifts up, and the other curves stay put
ATC shifts up but MC does not change
AFC and ATC shift up, but MC does not change
No curve shifts; the bakery moves along its curves

why.correct: A higher price of a variable input raises the cost of each extra unit (MC) and variable cost at each output (AVC), so ATC rises too. Fixed cost, and so AFC, is unchanged.
options: Right: flour is a variable cost, so every curve built on variable cost moves up.
Flour is not a fixed cost, so AFC is unchanged.
That is the effect of a higher fixed cost. Flour is used in every extra loaf, so MC rises too.
Flour is a variable cost: it raises MC, AVC and ATC, and leaves fixed cost and AFC as they were.
A change in an input price shifts cost curves; it is not a change in output.

items.q: In the graph, a firm is producing on the downward-sloping part of LRATC. If it builds a larger plant and produces more, its long-run average total cost will
options: rise, because a larger plant costs more in total
stay the same, because each input grew by the same share
