rise, because diminishing marginal returns set in
fall, because diseconomies of scale set in
fall, as it moves down the curve

why.correct: Left of minimum efficient scale, growing lowers long-run average total cost. That is the cost advantage of size in industries with large economies of scale.
options: Total cost rises, but it is spread over even more units, so the average falls here.
Equal growth in inputs can still lower cost per unit when there are economies of scale.
Diminishing returns need a fixed input; in the long run none is fixed.
Diseconomies of scale raise LRATC; on the falling part of the curve the firm has economies of scale.
Right: on the falling part, more output means a lower average cost.

items.q: How do diminishing marginal returns differ from diseconomies of scale?
options: They are two names for the same rise in cost
Diminishing returns happen in the long run; diseconomies in the short run
Diseconomies of scale come from rising input prices
One needs a fixed input; the other needs growth in each input
Diminishing returns lower costs; diseconomies raise them

why.correct: Diminishing marginal returns: in the short run, more of one input added to a fixed input. Diseconomies of scale: in the long run, all inputs grow and cost per unit rises, often from coordination problems.
options: Both raise costs, but they have different causes and time frames.
It is the other way round.
Diseconomies come from the strain of size, with input prices unchanged.
Right: one is a short-run idea, the other a long-run idea.
Both raise cost; the difference is that diminishing returns need a fixed input (short run) and diseconomies come from growing every input.

items.q: Use the table. Which firm shows an accounting profit but has an economic loss?
options: Firm X
Firms Y and Z
Firm Y
Firms X and Z
Firm Z

why.correct: Firm Z: accounting profit <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>300</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>200</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">300 - 200 = 100</annotation></semantics></math> thousand, but its implicit costs of 150 are larger, so economic profit is <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100 - 150 = -50</annotation></semantics></math> thousand: an economic loss.
options: Firm X has zero economic profit, not a loss.
Firm Y earns 400 - 250 - 100 = 50 above all costs, an economic profit, so only Firm Z fits; Firm Z’s implicit costs turn its accounting profit into an economic loss.
Firm Y earns a positive economic profit of 50 thousand.
Firm X has zero economic profit, which is not a loss.
Right: accounting profit 100, economic profit -50 thousand.

items.q: Which of these is an implicit cost for a dentist who owns her own practice?
options: The rent she pays for her office
The interest she pays on a loan for her chair
The salary she gave up at a hospital
The wages she pays her assistant
The bill for dental supplies

why.correct: An implicit cost is the value of something the owner already has (her time, her savings, her building) in its best other use; no money changes hands.
options: Rent is a payment: an explicit cost.
Interest she pays is money paid out, an explicit cost; the salary she gives up is the implicit one.
Right: forgone income is an opportunity cost with no payment.
Wages are paid out: an explicit cost.
A bill paid is an explicit cost.

items.q: Based on the table, what are Juniper's accounting profit and economic profit for the year?
options: Accounting profit $30,000; economic profit $10,000
Accounting loss $10,000; economic profit $30,000
Accounting profit $50,000; economic loss $10,000
Accounting profit $30,000; economic profit $70,000
Accounting profit $30,000; economic loss $10,000

why.correct: Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs only: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90{,}000 - 60{,}000</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= $30{,}000</annotation></semantics></math>. Economic profit also subtracts the implicit cost, the salary the owner gives up: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90{,}000 - 60{,}000 - 40{,}000</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -$10{,}000</annotation></semantics></math>, an economic loss.
options: Subtracting $40,000 from $30,000 leaves -$10,000: a loss, not a profit.
That swaps the two: accounting profit leaves out implicit costs, so it is the larger one.
Accounting profit subtracts the $60,000 of explicit costs, not the $40,000 implicit cost.
The forgone salary is a cost, so it is subtracted, not added.
Right: the owner's forgone salary turns an accounting profit into an economic loss.

items.q: Marginal revenue is
options: total revenue divided by the quantity sold
total revenue minus total cost
the extra cost of making one more unit
the price times the quantity sold
the extra revenue from one more unit

why.correct: Marginal revenue is the extra revenue from one more unit sold: the change in total revenue divided by the change in quantity.
options: That is average revenue.
That is profit.
That is marginal cost; marginal revenue is the extra revenue from selling one more unit.
That is total revenue.
Right: MR = ΔTR / ΔQ.

items.q: Use the table. Should the shop produce or shut down in the short run?
options: Produce: its price covers ATC at 100 jobs
Close: it loses money on each job
Produce: it loses $200, not $400
Close: the price is under the $12 ATC
Produce: it earns an economic profit of $200

why.correct: Compare the two losses: producing loses $200, shutting down loses the $400 fixed cost. Equivalently, P ($10) is above AVC, so produce.
options: ATC is $12 and the price $10, so it does not cover ATC; it produces because the price is above AVC, losing $200 rather than $400.
It loses $2 a job on average, but each job covers its variable cost and $2 of fixed cost.
Right: the price ($10) is above AVC ($8), so producing cuts the loss.
A price under ATC is a loss; closing would double it here.
It makes a loss of $200, not a profit.

items.q: Which part of a firm's MC curve is its short-run supply curve?
options: The part below the lowest point of AVC
The part above the lowest point of ATC
The whole MC curve, from zero output
The part where MC is falling
The part above the lowest point of AVC

why.correct: For any price above the lowest point of AVC, the firm produces where its MR line (the price) meets MC. Below that point it shuts down, so its supply is zero.
options: Below minimum AVC the firm shuts down and supplies nothing; the supply curve is MC above minimum AVC.
Between the AVC and ATC minimums the firm still supplies output, at a loss.
Below the AVC minimum the firm supplies nothing.
The firm produces on the rising part of MC.
Right: at each price above the shutdown point, the firm supplies where P = MR = MC.

items.q: In a constant-cost industry, what is the shape of the long-run industry supply curve?
options: Horizontal, at the lowest point of ATC
Upward sloping, like short-run market supply
Downward sloping, as larger firms get cheaper
Vertical, at the current market quantity
The same as the firm's MC curve

why.correct: When an industry grows or shrinks without changing its firms' costs, entry and exit bring the price back to the same lowest ATC, so long-run supply is horizontal at that price.
options: Right: after entry or exit the price returns to the same level.
In a constant-cost industry, a larger industry has the same costs, so the long-run price does not rise.
In a constant-cost industry, entry does not change input costs, so long-run supply is horizontal at minimum ATC.
Entry and exit change the quantity; the long-run supply curve is not vertical.
MC above AVC is one firm's short-run supply; long-run industry supply reflects entry and exit.

items.q: The graph shows a perfectly competitive market (left) and one firm in it (right), earning a loss, area a, and still producing. What happens in the long run?
options: Firms enter, market supply shifts right, and the price falls further
Market demand shifts right, because buyers see the low price
Firms exit, market supply shifts left, and the price rises to minimum ATC
Firms exit until the price rises to minimum AVC
The firm stays as it is, since it covers its variable cost

why.correct: With losses, some firms leave the industry. Market supply shifts left, the price rises, and exit goes on until the price reaches the lowest point of ATC, where the remaining firms earn zero economic profit.
options: Entry follows profits; a loss makes firms leave.
The low price is a movement along demand; the long-run change comes from exit shifting supply.
Right: exit ends when the loss is gone, at the lowest point of ATC.
At minimum AVC firms still make a loss; exit goes on until the price reaches minimum ATC.
Covering AVC is the short-run rule; in the long run every cost is variable, so firms leave if they make a loss.

items.q: What gives each salon in Market Z some market power?
options: Product differentiation: no rival offers quite the same style and location
Economies of scale that let one salon serve the whole county
A high barrier to entry that keeps new salons from opening nearby
A county license that lets it, and no other salon, cut hair
Agreement with the other salons on what each one will charge for a cut

why.correct: Product differentiation: each salon's style and location make it a little different, so some customers stay when it raises its price. That is why its demand curve slopes down even with forty rivals.
options: Right: differentiation lets a salon raise its price without losing every customer.
Salons are small and easy to open; their market power comes from differentiated styles and locations.
The description says a new salon can open in a few weeks, so entry is easy.
That describes Market X, not the salons.
Nothing in the description says the salons coordinate their prices.

items.q: A firm with market power earns positive economic profit year after year, while a perfectly competitive firm's economic profit returns to zero. What explains the difference?
options: The firm with market power has a lower marginal cost than rivals
Demand for its product keeps rising faster than costs over time
Barriers to entry keep rivals from competing the profit away
It produces where price equals marginal cost
Its demand is perfectly elastic at the market price

why.correct: In perfect competition, profit draws in new firms until it is gone. Barriers to entry stop new firms from entering, so a firm with market power can keep its economic profit in the long run.
options: Lower costs could raise profit for a while, but without barriers, entry would still compete it away.
Rising demand is not a reason profit lasts; entry would follow it.
Right: entry is what drives a competitive firm's profit to zero.
A firm with market power produces where MR = MC, and its price is above MC.
Perfectly elastic demand describes a price taker; profit lasts here because barriers to entry keep rivals out.

items.q: Which of the following is a barrier to entry?
options: Many buyers who are willing to pay a high price for the product
Low start-up costs, so a new firm needs little money to begin
A patent that makes one drug maker the sole seller of a medicine
A product that buyers can compare easily across sellers
A product that many firms can make with the same simple equipment

why.correct: A patent gives one firm the legal right to be the only seller of an invention for a period of years, so rivals cannot enter by copying it.
options: The number of buyers does not stop new sellers from entering.
Low start-up costs make entry easier, not harder.
Right: the law keeps other sellers out.
Easy comparison helps buyers switch, which does not keep rivals out; a patent gives one firm the legal right to sell.
An identical product that anyone can make invites entry.

items.q: A mining company owns every known deposit of a rare mineral used in batteries. What is the source of its market power?
options: Product differentiation from heavy advertising of its brand
A large number of small rivals
Economies of scale from its many small mines
A horizontal demand curve for its product
Control of a key resource that rivals cannot get

why.correct: Control of a key resource: no rival can produce the mineral without access to a deposit, so entry is blocked.
options: The mineral is the same whoever mines it; advertising is not what keeps rivals out.
Many rivals would reduce its market power.
Owning the key resource is what keeps rivals out here, not the size or number of its mines.
A horizontal demand curve would mean no market power at all.
Right: owning every deposit keeps rivals out.

items.q: A profit-maximizing monopolist with positive marginal cost produces on which part of its demand curve?
options: The inelastic part, where it can raise its price freely
The part where marginal revenue is negative
The elastic part, where marginal revenue is positive
The unit-elastic point, where total revenue is largest
The point where demand meets marginal cost

why.correct: At the profit-maximizing output MR = MC, and MC is positive, so MR is positive. Marginal revenue is positive only on the elastic part of a straight-line demand curve, above the unit-elastic midpoint.
options: On the inelastic part MR is negative; cutting output and raising the price would add revenue and cut costs.
Where MR is negative, cutting output would raise revenue and lower cost, so a monopolist with positive MC never stays there.
Right: MR = MC > 0, so the firm is above the unit-elastic point.
MR is zero there, which is below any positive MC.
That is the efficient quantity, larger than the monopoly quantity.

items.q: Compared with a perfectly competitive industry with the same costs, a monopoly
options: produces more and charges a higher price
produces less and charges a lower price
produces more and charges the same price
produces less and charges a higher price
produces the same amount at a higher price

why.correct: The monopolist restricts output to where MR = MC and charges a price above MC, so it produces less, charges more, and creates a deadweight loss.
options: A monopolist cuts output below the competitive quantity to raise its price.
Along a demand curve, less output goes with a higher price.
A monopoly restricts output to where MR = MC, below the competitive quantity, and so charges a higher price.
Right: MR = MC at a smaller quantity, with the price read from demand.
Output falls: the monopolist stops where MR = MC, short of P = MC.

items.q: Based on the table, what is Fallow Rail's economic profit for the year?
options: $300 thousand
$200 thousand
$1,000 thousand
$700 thousand
$100 thousand

why.correct: Profit is (price minus ATC) times quantity: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>5.00</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>3.50</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">($5.00 - $3.50) \times 200</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>300</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= $300</annotation></semantics></math> thousand. The price comes from the demand curve at the quantity where MR = MC.
options: Right: $1.50 a ride over ATC, on 200 thousand rides.
That uses MR ($4.50) as the price; the monopoly charges the price on the demand curve, $5.00.
That is total revenue, $5.00 times 200 thousand; profit subtracts total cost.
That is total cost, $3.50 times 200 thousand.
That uses MC instead of ATC; profit is price minus average total cost, times quantity.

items.q: Halloway dropped the student price and charged everyone $10. What would most likely happen to student ticket sales and to the cinema's profit?
options: Student sales would barely change and profit would rise
Student sales would rise, because the price is now the same for everyone
Student sales would rise and profit would stay the same
Student sales would fall sharply and profit would fall
Student sales would fall, but profit would rise by the full $4 a ticket

why.correct: Students' demand is elastic, so a much higher price would cut their purchases by a large share, and the lost student revenue and profit would not be made up. That is why separating the groups raises profit.
options: That would be true for inelastic demand; students' 2.5 is elastic.
A higher price lowers the quantity demanded.
Students’ demand is more elastic, so a higher price cuts their purchases sharply and the cinema loses that profit.
Right: elastic demand means a large drop in quantity, so the lost sales cost more than the higher price earns.
Fewer tickets are sold, so profit does not rise by $4 on each of the old sales.

items.q: The graph shows a monopolistically competitive firm earning an economic profit, area b. What happens in the long run?
options: Firms exit, its demand shifts right, and profit grows
The price falls until it equals MC at the lowest point of ATC
Its product differentiation keeps area b as profit in the long run
Firms enter, its demand shifts left until it is tangent to ATC, and profit falls to zero
Its costs rise until ATC meets demand, with demand unchanged

why.correct: Profit draws new firms with similar products. Each takes some of this firm's customers, so its demand (and MR) shifts left and becomes more elastic, until demand is tangent to ATC and economic profit is zero. Price stays above MC, and the firm produces less than at minimum ATC.
options: Profit draws firms in, not out.
That is the perfectly competitive long run; here price stays above MC and output is short of minimum ATC.
Entry is easy, so rivals with close substitutes compete the profit away.
Right: entry removes the profit; the firm ends with price equal to ATC, above MC.
The adjustment comes through demand: new rivals take customers and shift it left.

items.q: In an oligopoly, why does each firm need to think about its rivals' choices?
options: Each firm sells a product with no close substitutes
Each firm is a price taker that sells at the market price
There are so many firms that no one can affect the price
Each firm's choice changes its rivals' profits
Entry is easy, so new rivals arrive each week

why.correct: With only a few large firms, each one's price or output changes what the others earn: the firms are interdependent. That is why game theory is used to study oligopoly.
options: That describes a monopoly; oligopolists watch rivals because each firm’s choice changes the others’ profits.
Price takers ignore rivals; oligopolists cannot.
That describes perfect competition.
Right: interdependence is the mark of oligopoly.
Oligopolies usually have barriers to entry.

items.q: Based on the payoff matrix, which cells are Nash equilibria?
options: Marlo's late with Nessa's early, which has the largest joint profit, and no other cell
Marlo's early with Nessa's late, and Marlo's late with Nessa's early
There is no Nash equilibrium, because neither cafe has a dominant strategy
Both open early
Both open late

why.correct: In (Marlo's Early, Nessa's Late), Marlo's gets 12 rather than the 7 it would get by switching to Late, and Nessa's 9 rather than the 6 it would get by switching to Early, so neither gains by switching alone. In (Marlo's Late, Nessa's Early) the same holds: 10 > 8 for Marlo's and 12 > 5 for Nessa's. Neither cafe has a dominant strategy, but there are two Nash equilibria.
options: That cell is a Nash equilibrium, but so is (early, late); the largest joint profit does not make a cell the only one.
Right: in each, both cafes are playing a best response to the other.
A Nash equilibrium does not need a dominant strategy; check each cell for a profitable switch.
In that cell Marlo's would switch to late (10 > 8), so it is not a Nash equilibrium.
In that cell each cafe would switch to early (12 > 7 for Marlo's, 12 > 5 for Nessa's).

items.q: Why is a firm's MRP curve its demand curve for labor?
options: It shows the wage the firm pays each worker
It shows how many people want to work at each wage
It shows the firm's total cost of hiring each number of workers
It shows how much output each worker makes on average
It shows what each added worker is worth to the firm

why.correct: At a given wage, the firm keeps hiring while a worker adds at least that much revenue. So the MRP schedule tells how many workers the firm wants at each wage: its demand for labor.
options: The wage is set in the labor market; the MRP curve shows each added worker’s value to the firm, which is why it is labor demand.
That describes the people offering to work, the sellers in the market, not the firm.
Costs are a different curve; MRP measures revenue added by each worker.
That is average product, not the extra revenue from one more worker.
Right: a firm is willing to pay up to a worker's MRP, so the MRP curve gives the quantity of labor it wants at each wage.

items.q: A new machine lets each of a firm's workers produce more output. The product price does not change. What happens to the MRP of each worker?
options: It falls, because the machine replaces some workers
It falls, because the firm needs fewer hours of work
It rises, because each worker's marginal product rises
It stays the same, because the price of the product is unchanged
It rises, because the price of the product rises

why.correct: Higher productivity raises marginal product at each quantity of labor, so MRP rises even with the same product price.
options: The question says each worker makes more; that raises MP and MRP at each quantity of labor.
MRP is marginal product times marginal revenue; the machine raises each worker’s marginal product, so MRP rises.
Right: MRP = MP × MR, and MP is higher at every number of workers.
MRP depends on MP as well as the price; a rise in MP raises MRP.
The price is unchanged here; MRP rises through marginal product.

items.q: The price of a good falls, and nothing else changes. What happens to the marginal revenue product of the workers who make it?
options: It falls at every quantity of labor
It rises, because the good is cheaper to make
It falls for the last worker and stays the same for the rest
It stays the same, because marginal product is unchanged
It falls for the first worker and rises for the others

why.correct: For a competitive seller MRP = MP × P. A lower P lowers MRP for every worker.
options: Right: each worker makes the same output, but each unit now brings in less revenue.
A lower selling price lowers revenue per unit; it says nothing about cost.
MRP is marginal product times marginal revenue; a lower price lowers marginal revenue, so MRP falls for every worker.
MRP = MP × MR; with MR lower, MRP falls even though MP is the same.
The lower price lowers the revenue from every worker's output.

items.q: Delivery drones and drivers are complements for a parcel company: each drone needs a driver to load it. Drones become much cheaper. What happens to the demand for drivers?
options: It decreases
It increases at first and then falls below where it began
It does not change
It increases
Labor supply decreases instead

why.correct: A cheaper complementary input leads firms to use more of it, and more of the labor that goes with it.
options: That would be true if drones replaced drivers. Here they are used together.
Cheaper drones mean more drones, each needing a driver, so demand for the complement, drivers, rises; nothing here turns it back down.
The price of a complementary input shifts labor demand.
Right: the company buys more drones, and each needs a driver.
The change is on the company's side: the demand for drivers.

items.q: Why does a firm's marginal factor cost of labor equal the wage when the labor market is perfectly competitive?
options: The firm pays each worker the MRP of that worker
Each added worker produces as much as the one before
The firm sets the wage for its own workers
The wage falls as the firm hires more workers
Each added worker is hired at the same market wage

why.correct: For a wage taker, MFC = change in total labor cost ÷ change in workers = W.
options: Workers are paid the market wage, not their MRP.
Output per worker is about MRP, not about cost.
A firm in a competitive labor market is a wage taker; it pays the market wage for each added worker, so MFC equals the wage.
A wage taker hires any number at the same wage.
Right: so total labor cost rises by exactly the wage with each worker.

items.q: In the graph, compared with a perfectly competitive labor market with the same MRP and SL curves, the monopsony
options: hires fewer workers and pays a higher wage
hires more workers and pays a higher wage
hires more workers and pays a lower wage
hires the same number of workers and pays a lower wage
hires fewer workers and pays a lower wage

why.correct: Each extra hire raises the pay of every worker, so the monopsonist hires less than a competitive market would and pays less.
options: A smaller quantity on an upward-sloping SL means a lower wage, not a higher one.
The monopsonist hires where MRP = MFC, to the left of the competitive quantity, and pays the lower wage read from labor supply.
MFC lies above SL, so the monopsony stops sooner.
Its quantity is where MRP = MFC, which is less than where MRP = SL.
Right: it stops where MRP = MFC, to the left of where MRP meets SL, and pays the lower wage on SL.

items.q: The hospital pays every technician the same wage. Based on the table, how many technicians does it hire to maximize profit, and at what wage?
options: 3 technicians at $18 an hour
4 technicians at $14 an hour
3 technicians at $16 an hour
2 technicians at $10 an hour
3 technicians at $12 an hour

why.correct: Total labor cost is $8, $20, $36 and $56, so MFC is $8, $12, $16 and $20. The hospital hires while MRP is at least MFC: the third technician adds $18 of revenue for $16 of cost, the fourth $14 for $20. It hires 3 and pays the wage labor supply needs for 3: $12.
options: The number is right, but a monopsonist pays the wage on labor supply, not the MRP.
That is the competitive outcome, where MRP meets the wage; the monopsonist compares MRP with MFC, which is higher than the wage.
That is the MFC of the third technician; the wage paid is read from labor supply.
The third technician adds $18 of revenue for $16 of cost, so hiring stops at 3, not 2.
Right: MRP <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>≥</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math> MFC up to 3, and the wage comes from labor supply.

items.q: In the graph, demand is the marginal social benefit of bus rides and supply the marginal social cost. Which area is the deadweight loss of the subsidy?
options: Areas b, c, e, f and g
Areas b and c
Area c
Area g
Area a

why.correct: The units beyond the efficient quantity cost more to make (MSC) than they are worth to buyers (MSB); the gap summed over those units is area g.
options: That is the cost of the subsidy to the government, most of which goes to buyers and sellers.
Areas b and c are part of the subsidy’s cost that goes to buyers and sellers; the deadweight loss is the triangle g past the efficient quantity.
Area c is a gain to buyers from the lower price.
Right: the triangle between supply and demand beyond the original equilibrium, out to the new quantity.
Area a is consumer surplus before the subsidy.

items.q: A competitive market with no effects on anyone else is at equilibrium. A binding price floor is then set. What happens to efficiency?
options: Efficiency rises, because sellers earn more per unit
Deadweight loss appears, because less is bought than the efficient quantity
Nothing changes, because supply and demand do not shift
Efficiency rises, because the floor ends the shortage
Deadweight loss appears, because more is bought than the efficient quantity

why.correct: A binding floor moves the quantity traded away from MSB = MSC, so total surplus falls.
options: Higher prices for sellers are a transfer; the lost units are a loss.
Right: at the floor, quantity demanded falls below the efficient quantity.
The quantity traded changes even though the curves do not.
A binding floor sits above equilibrium and creates a surplus, not a shortage; trade falls below the efficient quantity.
At a price above equilibrium, buyers buy less, not more.

items.q: Which statement about a negative production externality is correct?
options: The market price is too high and the quantity too low
The market price is too low and the quantity too high
MSC lies below MPC
Demand lies above MSB
MPC lies above MSC, so the quantity is too low

why.correct: Negative production externality: MSC > MPC, market Q > efficient Q, market P < efficient P.
options: That is the pattern of a positive production externality.
Right: firms do not pay the external cost, so supply is too far right.
With a negative production externality MSC lies above MPC.
The externality is on the cost side; here demand equals MSB.
With a negative production externality MSC is above MPC, and the market overproduces at too low a price.

items.q: A toll road is uncrowded, so one more car does not slow anyone down, and drivers who do not pay are stopped at the gate. What kind of good is the road?
options: A club good
A public good
A rival good, because each car uses up road space
A common resource
A private good

why.correct: Excludable and nonrival goods can be sold by firms, often with a membership or entry fee.
options: Right: nonrival (while uncrowded) and excludable.
The gate makes it excludable.
One more car slows no one, so the uncrowded road is nonrival; the toll gate makes it excludable: a club good.

items.q: A government pays a monopoly a per-unit subsidy. Compared with no subsidy, what happens to the monopoly's output?
options: It stays the same, because a monopoly sets its own output
It falls, because the subsidy raises its fixed cost
It rises, because the subsidy lowers marginal cost
It falls, because the monopoly earns more profit
It stays the same, because the subsidy is a lump sum

why.correct: Per-unit taxes and subsidies change MC and so output; lump-sum ones change only profit.
options: A change in MC changes the profit-maximizing output.
A per-unit subsidy lowers marginal cost, so MR meets MC at a larger quantity: output rises.
Right: MC shifts down, so MR = MC at a larger quantity.
More profit per unit gives a reason to produce more, not less.
A per-unit subsidy depends on output, so it changes marginal cost.

items.q: On Talmora's Lorenz curve, what percent of income do the lowest 40 percent of households receive?

why.correct: A Lorenz curve is cumulative: the lowest 40 percent are the lowest two fifths, with <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\% + 9\% = 13\%</annotation></semantics></math> of income. With perfect equality they would have 40 percent.
options: That is the second fifth alone; the curve adds up the shares from the bottom.
That is where the line of equality would be.
Right: the lowest fifth plus the second fifth.
That adds the lowest three fifths: the lowest 60 percent.
That is the share of the highest fifth.
